To corner means to trap someone or something so they have no escape and no good options left. Think of a literal corner in a room — it's a closed-off space where you can't move forward, left, or right. When you corner someone, you recreate that feeling for them, either physically or in a broader sense.

The person doing the cornering has power and control. The person being cornered is stuck.

To corner a person or animal is to chase or maneuver them into a place — a dead end, an enclosed space, a wall — where they physically cannot escape.

"The police cornered the suspect in a narrow alley."
"The dog cornered the cat under the staircase."

The key here is movement: you position yourself or use barriers so the other person or creature has nowhere to go.

This is one of the most common everyday uses. To corner someone socially means to catch them in a situation where they can't easily walk away, often because you want to talk to them about something — especially something they'd rather avoid.

"She cornered him at the office party and demanded to know why he hadn't replied to her emails."
"He keeps trying to corner me after class to discuss extra work."

There's usually a slight sense of pressure or persistence here — the person being cornered didn't exactly choose the conversation. It's not violent or dramatic, but there's an edge of discomfort. You've caught them when they can't escape without being rude.
3. Putting Someone in an Impossible Position — in Argument or Logic

You can corner someone intellectually. This means using questions, evidence, or logic to put them in a position where any answer they give will hurt them — they have no good move left.

"The lawyer cornered the witness by asking the one question that exposed the contradiction in his story."
"The journalist cornered the minister with a series of facts he couldn't explain away."

Think of it like a chess move that leaves your opponent with no good response. You've backed them into a logical or rhetorical corner.

This is a specific and well-established use in business and economics. To corner a market means to gain control over so much of the supply of a particular product or resource that other buyers have nowhere else to go — you've trapped the entire market and can now dictate the price.

"In the 1800s, powerful traders sometimes tried to corner the silver market."
"The company's strategy was to corner the market on a rare mineral before its competitors noticed it."

The same logic applies: you've removed everyone's options. The "corner" here is not a physical place but a position of total control — no exits, no alternatives, no escape for anyone else.

Interestingly, you can also corner yourself — through your own choices, lies, or mistakes, you end up in a situation with no good way out.

"By promising different things to different people, she had cornered herself — there was no story that would satisfy everyone."
"He cornered himself with his own lies."

Here, no one trapped you — your own actions created the inescapable situation.

"To be cornered" is extremely common and worth learning as its own natural expression.

"She felt completely cornered — whatever she said would upset someone."
"He was cornered with no honest answer to give."

And there's a very important phrase: "when cornered." This is used to describe what someone does when they're trapped with no good options.

"When cornered, he always resorted to anger."
"Like many politicians, when cornered, she deflected."

There's a powerful and widely used idea that comes directly from this verb: a cornered animal is the most dangerous kind. When an animal (or a person) has been cornered and has no escape, they often stop trying to flee and start fighting desperately — because they have nothing left to lose. You'll encounter this in many forms:

"Don't corner him — a desperate man is unpredictable."
"He fought back ferociously, like a cornered animal."

This idea — that removing someone's options doesn't make them submit, it makes them dangerous — is embedded in how the word is used across politics, psychology, and everyday life.
The Emotional and Strategic Flavour of the Word

Whenever you see "corner" used as a verb, remember these qualities are almost always present:

  • Control and power — the one doing the cornering has the upper hand.
  • Loss of freedom — the one being cornered has had their options taken away.
  • Pressure and discomfort — being cornered rarely feels neutral; it feels threatening or uncomfortable.
  • Intentionality — cornering is usually done on purpose. Someone engineers the trap.

Whether it's a detective cornering a suspect, a journalist cornering a politician, a company cornering a market, or someone cornering you at a social event to talk about something awkward — the verb always carries that same essential force: your escape routes are gone.
